title: Mentoring Junior Engineers as a Senior
description: How senior backend engineers build real mentoring instincts beyond code review comments and 1:1s
linkedin_post:
The hardest part of becoming a senior engineer isn't the technical depth. It's learning how to transfer it.

Most engineers get promoted to senior because they ship reliably, debug well, and make sound design calls. But the expectation quietly shifts: now you're supposed to help others do those things. And nobody really teaches you how.

A few things I've seen separate engineers who mentor well from those who don't:

— They resist solving the problem immediately. They ask what the other person has already tried and why. This slows the moment but builds the habit.

— They share context, not just conclusions. "Use a worker pool here" is less useful than explaining what problem unbounded goroutines actually create in production under load.

— They treat code review as teaching, not gatekeeping. Comments that explain the tradeoff land differently than comments that just request a change.

— They notice when someone is stuck on confidence, not capability. Sometimes the blocker isn't technical. A senior engineer who can tell the difference changes the trajectory of that person's career.

What makes this hard is that good mentoring is often invisible. The junior engineer solves it. The PR ships. Nobody sees the conversation that made it possible.

But the compounding effect is real. Teams where senior engineers mentor well tend to debug faster, make fewer repeated mistakes, and produce stronger technical proposals over time. The floor of the whole team rises.

If you're at the senior level, the question worth sitting with isn't just what are you building — it's who are you building up?

What's one mentoring habit that actually made a difference in your experience — giving or receiving?
